item.title: TimeTeller puts our internal clocks at the center of personalized medicine
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
At-home health testing has been mired in overblown claims and outright fraud. But German startup TimeTeller, which has developed a saliva test kit to help anyone understand their circadian rhythm, is led by CEO Angela Relógio, who is the polar opposite of Theranos’ disgraced founder Elizabeth Holmes. Relógio is a physicist-engineer and molecular biologist who spent years researching oncology, circadian biology, and systems medicine in Germany before leaving academia to build TimeTeller. She is careful about what the test can and can’t do today. It would be easy to oversell: Relógio’s last name means “clock” in her native Portuguese, and TimeTeller has the potential to reduce side effects from cancer treatment and improve outcomes by timing treatment to each patient’s internal clock. That’s also why she’s careful to warn that TimeTeller itself operates on two timelines. The long-term goal is to determine when cancer treatments will be better tolerated and most effective, and doing so much more granularly than just telling whether someone is a morning person or a night owl. But its direct-to-consumer kit won’t help patients figure that out on their own. “That is something that we need to calculate for every single medicine; we do that in the context of clinical studies,” Relógio cautioned. According to Relógio, TimeTeller started accepting direct orders because of demand from longevity clinics, which focus on healthy aging and understand that individual data on a person’s circadian rhythm can be used to offer personalized advice on sleep, nutrition, light exposure, and physical activity. TimeTeller could also apply to metabolic diseases (such as diabetes) and neurodegenerative diseases (such as Alzheimer’s), performance, and women’s health, but cancer is its core mission. It was while studying cancer that Relógio made the discovery that led her to leave academia. She noticed that many cancer patients stopped or started their treatment because of side effects. “As a scientist, that was just impossible to watch, particularly when I was convinced that part of the problem might not only be what treatment we give, but when we give it,” Relógio said. This led her to develop the circadian rhythm test at the core of TimeTeller — which she knew had to become a company. “I personally funded our first patent because I strongly believed that this discovery should not remain in scientific publications,” she said. The startup spun out of Berlin’s Charité university hospital but has since moved to Medical School Hamburg, which provided access to patients and funding. It also offered a fallback: backup employment for TimeTeller’s team of 10 if the company couldn’t pay them. That’s a safety net TimeTeller may not need. Having enlisted biochemist and market access specialist Benjamin Dose as a co-founder, the startup secured a partnership with Techniker Krankenkasse, one of Germany’s largest health insurance providers. The partnership started out as a reimbursement deal in which the insurer pays back the cost of the test for a subset of cancer patients, and both sides are now ready to expand it to more of the insurer’s 12 million members, Relógio said. Despite her caveats about the direct-to-consumer test, TimeTeller has become a solution that cancer patients can actually access. Ahead of her appearance at TechCrunch Disrupt, where Relógio appeared onstage today in San Francisco as part of our storied Startup Battlefield competition, she made clear that the company has broader ambitions: a future in which asking “when” is central to precision medicine, because “almost every process in our body is timed.” You aren’t too late to join the action at Disrupt. Come for the headliners; stay to see who wins this year’s no-strings check from TechCrunch — and the attention of the hundreds of VCs in attendance.

item.title: Brain Drain Is a Bigger Threat to National Cybersecurity Than AI
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
Whether we’d admit it or not, most of us by now have offloaded some cognitive effort onto AI. Chatbots and agents have become so commonplace that it’s often tricky to avoid them. The stakes of this use are usually pretty low; we may compromise some of our own critical thinking skills and creativity in the process, but the harm stops there. In some cases, however, an over-reliance on automation can have major downstream consequences. Cybersecurity is the most notable example. Thankfully, that’s a field that most of us almost never have to think about, because most of the time, the computer systems running critical infrastructure—from water treatment facilities to the stock market—function as they’re supposed to. But many of those systems haven’t been updated in decades. In July of last year, a report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that the Department of Defense’s in-house IT system has been in use since before the first Apollo moon landing. (The Department of the Treasury and the Environmental Protection Agency weren’t far behind.) “These agencies’ missions are essential to government operations such as health care, critical infrastructure, tax processing, and national security, and these legacy systems provide vital support to the agencies’ missions,” the GAO wrote in its report. COBOL, a computer programming language invented in 1959, is still widely used on IBM mainframe computers across the U.S. government, so much so that during the pandemic the governor of New Jersey was forced to put out a call for “cobalt” (his word) programmers to help maintain the state’s decrepit, aged, and overwhelmed unemployment system. Unfortunately for the cybersecurity of the United States, much has changed since those “legacy” cybersecurity systems were first installed. Programmers today—perhaps more than any other profession—rely on AI in their day-to-day work. And while that may have led to some efficiency gains, it’s also turned much of modern programming itself into a black box. In a recent study with over 50 (mostly junior) software engineers, Anthropic found that using AI for coding “led to a statistically significant decrease in mastery.” And in a May survey of more than 850 cybersecurity professionals, two-thirds of them said they were now spending more of their time on the job reviewing AI outputs and trying to decide whether to trust them or not. Much of modern cybersecurity, in other words, revolves around just trying to interpret AI. Meanwhile, leading AI companies have been competing to build what are effectively autonomous cybersecurity locksmiths. Anthropic’s Mythos, which the company first announced in April, was deemed to be so frighteningly good at finding and exploiting cyber vulnerabilities in software that the company said it would not initially release it to the public, choosing instead to roll it out gradually to a group of handpicked partners. The wide-eyed, almost reverent secrecy with which Anthropic teased the model quickly turned it into a cybersecurity bogeyman. In its own tests, the NSA—widely considered to be the Fort Knox of cybersecurity—reportedly used Mythos to discover flaws in its own system within a matter of hours. Other labs, like OpenAI and Google, soon followed up with their own models, which were described as being potentially dangerous hacking tools if they were allowed to fall into the wrong hands. (And in many cases, most notably the July Hugging Face hack, AI models from frontier companies didn’t even need human operators to commit cybercrimes.) While there were those who brushed fears of an AI-triggered cybercatastrophe aside as doomerism or marketing hype, plenty of experts were genuinely worried. In June, the Five Eyes—an alliance comprising the government intelligence agencies in the U.S., Canada, U.K., Australia, and New Zealand—warned that the new fleet of AI models arriving on the market “are anticipated to exceed current industry expectations, fundamentally transforming both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities. The timeline is not years; it is months.” Indeed, the cybersecurity threat posed by buzzy new models like Mythos and OpenAI’s Astra has dominated the public spotlight so much that it’s arguably blinded us to some much more subtle—but no less consequential—events unfolding in the wings. While the IT systems running critical U.S. government infrastructure have grown a bit long in the tooth, there’s been a simultaneous exodus of the very seasoned professionals who know how to operate and manage those legacy systems. Factor in an incoming generation of engineering talent that’s become largely dependent on AI assistance and you have a potentially explosive situation, experts say. “There is a brain drain from the federal government at the very time when the cybersecurity challenges are a mess,” Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Center for Technology Innovation at the Brookings Institute, told Gizmodo. Take the U.S. Cybersecurity and Information Security Agency (CISA), for example. Folded within the Department of Homeland Security, Trump inaugurated the agency during his first term to “lead the national effort to understand, manage, and reduce risk to our cyber and physical infrastructure,” according to its website. Alas, part of that infrastructure includes the U.S. voting system, which meant Trump had some qualms with the agency after losing the 2020 election to Joe Biden, a loss he has yet to publicly concede; Trump fired Christopher Krebs, then director of CISA, before leaving office in January 2021. After Trump regained the presidency in 2024, his new administration—guided by Elon Musk’s short-lived Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)—began slashing CISA’s budget, producing a surge of layoffs. Many of the agency’s outgoing officials had spent long stretches of their careers updating and fortifying the federal government’s cybersecurity systems during a period of profound technological change, marked first by the rise of the internet and followed by social media. According to Josephine Wolff, a professor of cybersecurity policy at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy at Tufts University, the result was a sudden and dramatic loss of hard-won expertise. “It’s a little heartbreaking when you think back over the past twenty or so years how much time, energy, and effort went into trying to build up cybersecurity expertise on the civilian side,” says Wolff. “I don’t know how long it will take to restore [that].” It could be a long time, considering the difficulties that government agencies already have trying to attract and retain new cybersecurity talent, competing with high-paying private sector roles on the one hand and navigating federal budget cuts on the other. According to one survey conducted earlier this year, more than half of all government agencies across the country—not just federal but also state and municipal—have been struggling with cybersecurity recruitment and churn. The drying up of an incoming domestic pipeline coupled with a federal immigration crackdown on foreign talent “is a catastrophic combination” for U.S. cybersecurity, says West. Without a steady flow of incoming cybersecurity engineers and experienced professionals to train them on the intricacies of the government’s antiquated system, that system could become more and more opaque, leading to greater and greater vulnerability for critical infrastructure. AI may be able to serve as a makeshift middleman between federal employees and their IT systems, but that’s not going to fix the underlying problems. This is one of those problems where just ignoring it is only going to make it worse, especially with an administration that’s ratcheting up its belligerence overseas; while CISA’s coffers have been depleted, the Pentagon’s have swelled. “You’re not safer by going out into the world and punching everyone else in the face—actually that’ll make you significantly less safe, unless you’re willing to actually defend yourself at the same time,” says Safa Shahwan Edwards, director of the Cyber Statecraft Initiative at the Atlantic Council, a think tank based in Washington D.C. “So having all those investments in offense and not making the requisite investments in defense, and not giving CISA the resources that they need to do their jobs well… I don’t know what’s going to happen. It’s not going to be good.”

item.title: How to improve your online privacy and security in Google Chrome
item.description:
Source: Engadget
How to improve your online privacy and security in Google Chrome Google has a vested interest in collecting and selling your data, but that doesn't mean protecting yourself is impossible. Google Chrome is easily the biggest browser in the game — and the hottest commodity in that game is data. Whenever you surf the web, your personal data becomes a product, whether you surrender it willingly or unknowingly to any number of vendors, or a hacker slips through the cracks and makes off with your information. Fortunately, there are many ways to secure your Google account, and not just with Chrome's new fortnightly updates. Of course, when it comes to privacy, using Chrome might be starting off on the wrong foot. While it has many upsides in terms of security, Google's privacy measures are flawed compared to a browser like Firefox; your Google account collects a great deal of day-to-day information about you, including app usage and browser history. However, if you're already set up with Google, there are some measures you can take to improve your security. Improving your privacy settings in Google Chrome First things first, head to the three dots in the top right of your browser, scroll down to Settings and head to Privacy and security. Right away, you'll want to tap on Third-party cookies and select Block third-party cookies, then turn on Do Not Track. The latter is only a request, so sites that receive the request when you enter them can choose to acknowledge or ignore that request at their own discretion. Before looking at more settings in this area, there are more privacy-specific toggles to be checked elsewhere. If you click on your Google profile icon instead of the three dots and navigate to Manage your Google Account > Data & privacy, you can toggle off Web & App Activity, which is another setting Google uses to extract more of your data. Once you've done that, you can also turn off Timeline, which is the setting Google uses to track your location history, as well as Personalize Search, which collects data to tailor search results and AI responses to your activity. To further depersonalize ads (meaning more protection for your data from Google's modus operandi), you can turn off personalized ads in My Ad Center. Turning attention to security, whether it's Chrome's Gemini Nano scam protection or its Safety Check review system, the browser is much more robust here than with privacy. First, head back to the three-dot menu > Settings > Privacy and security, where you can click on Go to Safety Check, which will scan for any security issues you might have and tell you how to resolve them. In addition to any immediate problems, it will let you know if you're reusing any passwords too much and if you need a Chrome update. Chrome's Safety Check will also constantly run in the background, keeping you alert to threats as they arise. While you're in the Privacy and security zone, you should take a gander at the Safe Browsing section. There are three types of Safe Browsing, with the default Standard protection standing constant vigil against potentially dangerous websites, downloads and extensions. Here, you can turn on Enhanced protection to add an AI-powered layer of security to your searching, though it's fine to forgo if you're not fond of AI-charged zealotry. Right below that, you can also turn on Always use secure connections, which will grant an advance warning if a site doesn't support secure connections.

item.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon. Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security, says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said. Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet. Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach. Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense. Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating. That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts. When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway. “In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.” Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying. “We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said. In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools. To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do. What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation. “We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained. The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium, a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers. She said 70% of Pluto’s sales pipeline now comes from inbound interest, although she didn’t break down how much of that comes directly through Plutonium. Pluto said it plans to invest the new capital in developing its product, expanding its security research efforts, and growing its presence in the U.S. It has 40 employees in the U.S. and Israel.

item.title: Your PC's Built-In Security Isn't Enough: How to Pick the Real Antivirus You Need
item.description:
Source: PCMag
When your PC was new, it almost certainly had a trial version of some antivirus software preinstalled. If you allowed that trial to expire, your protection reverted to the built-in Microsoft Defender Antivirus. Defender is better than nothing, but as I frequently report, it’s not sufficient protection. If you're ready to step up to a standalone third-party antivirus, the challenge isn't finding options—it's figuring out which one actually fits your setup and budget. I've been testing antivirus software since the 1980s, and I'm here to simplify your decision by cutting through the fluff and focusing on what actually matters. 5 Non-Negotiable Features Your Antivirus Needs There are some features that every serious antivirus absolutely must have: - On-demand scanning: This lets you manually check specific files, folders, or drives whenever you want. - Scheduled scanning: Automatically sweep your system for hidden threats at set intervals. - Real-time execution checks: Inspect every application for malicious code the moment before it launches. - Malware URL blocking: Stop your browser from connecting to known dangerous domains and malicious links. - Phishing protection: This identifies and redirects you away from fraudulent websites trying to steal credentials. The good news is that almost all antivirus apps cover these essentials, so there's no reason to choose a product that falls short. How Much Should You Spend? (Spoiler: Free Options Work) With a few exceptions, most antivirus apps fall into three price areas for a single installation. You can pay just under $40, $50, or $60. And yes, there are excellent choices at all three price points. Editors' Choice winner Norton AntiVirus Plus runs $59.99 for a single license, and Bitdefender Antivirus Plus, another Editors' Choice winner, costs $49.99. There are plenty of admirable four-star antivirus apps in the $40 range. There’s every chance you need to protect more than one computer, though. Most five-device licenses cost between $50 and $100 annually. Fewer antiviruses come with a 10-license option, but those that do range from $60 to almost $170. There are even a handful of apps with an unlimited license tier. Of course, none of these pricing figures matter if your budget doesn’t include an allowance for security. Fortunately, there are quite a few free antivirus options, many of which are quite effective, and you can check out our top picks here. Bonus Features: Which Ones Are Worth Paying For (and Which to Skip) Some antivirus apps check off all the essentials described above and stop there, doing everything that’s required without extra features. Others pile on anywhere from a handful of bonus features to a huge collection that rivals some security suites. Some popular bonus features are a direct extension of the antivirus basics: - Detection of operating system exploits and vulnerabilities - Scanning for apps that are missing important security patches - Dedicated support for virus infections (if malware gets past the antivirus, tech support experts will log in remotely and fix the problem) Other bonuses are security-related, but not truly part of antivirus essentials: - Red and green highlights that mark search results as dangerous or safe - A personal firewall, to defend against network-based attacks It’s true that firewall protection is more commonly seen as the heart of a security suite, paired with antivirus software. Some antivirus apps pack in additional suite components, such as: - File shredding (secure deletion) Now, though, let’s take a step back. It’s easy to be dazzled by an antivirus with a huge array of security features, but will you truly put all those features to use? When choosing among several antivirus apps, make a list of the bonus features each offers. Then highlight features that you think you’ll use and cross out ones that you know you won’t. This little exercise can help narrow down your choices, especially if the options hit different price points.

item.title: The more I learn about password security, the simpler my passwords get
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
The more leaks and hacks in the news, the more I find myself wondering—what’s the ideal password? For years, I’ve based my definition off expert advice. You want long, random, unique. But lately I’ve thought the answer is actually less specific than that. I’d say the ideal password is simple—while still strong, too. And what fits that definition can change depending on the context. Hear me out. Welcome to Safe Mode, your weekly report for pressing security and privacy news—and what steps to take next. Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website! In some cases, the ideal password is actually a passkey. (So not a password at all.) They’re the epitome of simple and secure. No memorization and not reusable, with baked-in elements of two-factor authentication. For these reasons, I recommend their use first to most people. Meanwhile for websites that lack passkey support, an ideal password is indeed something long, random, and unique—something easily generated and stored by a password manager. You’ll spend as little effort on a 32-character password as you would an 8-character version. But what about when you actually have to memorize a password? My opinion has shifted most on the approach here. You should memorize at least a handful—at minimum two passwords, one for your password manager and the other for your email address. You don’t want to find yourself locked out of your email address or another important account (e.g., banking) because you lost access to your password manager. Doing so shouldn’t feel hard, though. I used to equally suggest passphrases and pseudo-randomization (e.g., pulling the 2nd letter from song lyrics you know and interspersing numbers and special characters). Now I’m much more in the passphrase camp. The longer, the better. If you’re capable of memorizing a random mix of words, bonus points. What changed my mind: Looking once again at password cracking charts. Cybersecurity firms sometimes put out this info—one company, Hive Systems, does a whole set that looks at how easily consumer-grade PC hardware can crack passwords. This year’s data was a good reminder of not just the basics, but where the bar realistically sits, too. (The basics: Your password instantly gets cracked for anything stolen in a breach, reused on multiple sites, or commonly used dictionary words.) An eight-character password—the bare minimum requirement for websites now—takes 12 years for a fleet of 16 Nvidia RTX 5090 graphics cards to crack, if you use a mix of just upper and lowercase letters. Add in numbers, and that time rises to 50 years. Slap in special characters, and that collective of high-powered GPUs need 132 years. So it is it strictly necessary to have a super long password? No. Is it still a good idea? Absolutely, because you don’t know what will happen to your password information if it ever leaks. But when you must memorize a password, prioritize one that’s good enough and will stick in your head. It’ll trump one that’s perfect but forgettable, especially if you pair it with two-factor authentication. Better to chop off a few characters from a password’s length and go for a double layer approach to account protection—you’ll have a better chance at resisting an account takeover attempt. You might not even have to choose between length and strength, if you choose a passphrase with more than four words. With how complicated cybersecurity is right now, I’m all about going the easier (yet still well-protected) route. I wrote about Meta’s Muse personal agent at length last week, and how I didn’t trust it with access to my digital life. Turns out my mistrust was wise—yet another major privacy goof happened, with a Muse user realizing the agent had shared his home address with a stranger. Just keep saying no, folks. (At least for now.) - Apple reacted quickly to reports that Meta’s Muse AI agent can access data on macOS that it wasn’t explicit permitted to see—the Cupertino company says it will change how full disk access works, to better curtail nosy AI agents. - Certain AI agents can be manipulated into spreading malicious behavior to other agents in their network. The problem: Agents used for specific tasks have fewer restrictions and safeties applied to them. Poison one, possibly poison many others. All thanks to laxness in how these agents communicate with one another. - Meta Muse kept hitting the news for disappointing reasons—in this case, an uncomfortable scenario where the AI agent sent a stranger to a user’s home. Muse thought to help sell an item. The user got a nasty surprise when they realized the would-be buyer had shown up and left without them knowing. You may do a digital refresh of your phone and PC every so often—getting rid of photos and documents you don’t want to hog storage space—but have you also done a similar clean-up of your apps? On your devices, periodically uninstall apps and browser extensions you no longer use daily. Why? Legitimate software no longer is a good protection against malware. Sometimes, that “good” app you have could turn dark, if the developer sells it to a shady person…or is just hacked by one.

item.title: Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
item.description:
Source: The Verge
Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO’s secretive robotics project. Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president Ford’s former EV and software chief will run Rivian’s robotics startup at a time of maximum hype for physical AI. Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company’s ultimately unsuccessful Project Titan effort to make an autonomous electric car. He had a previous stint at Apple as VP of Mac hardware engineering, but he left the company in 2013 to become Tesla’s chief vehicle engineer, where he helped oversee the Model 3 sedan. He left Tesla in 2018 and rejoined Apple. In 2021, Field was hired by Ford to run the automaker’s electric vehicle and software division, a position he held until earlier this year. Mind Robotics said Field will oversee its effort to build “universally capable robots” for the purpose of working in Rivian’s factories, as well as other applications. The startup was founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe in 2025, and has since raised over $1 billion in financing. While the company has yet to show off any of its robots in public, the startup says its robots are being designed with “dexterity and physical reasoning” that’s required for industrial work. “Doug is a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products, and I couldn’t be more excited to be building Mind with him,” Scaringe said in a statement. “He has an incredible ability to foster great teams that take on big, complex ideas and deliver products that reset expectations. That’s exactly what Mind needs as we deploy robots into real factories and beyond.” Field joins Mind Robotics at a major turning point for the field of robotics, with rapid advances in physical AI colliding with major hurdles in hardware and software development. Several companies, like Tesla and Hyundai, are pursuing humanoid robots for factory and warehouse work — even as experts note that making a robot act like a human is easier than scaling the technology for practical work. Mind Robotics hasn’t confirmed whether it’s working on a humanoid design or something else entirely. The company has been on a hiring spree and currently has 32 open positions. Scaringe, who serves as acting CEO and chair of Mind Robotics, has said he wants to keep the companies separate, rather than try to combine the work like Tesla. That said, the companies are certainly linked in several ways. Mind Robotics is using AI training data from Rivian, and the robots will be initially tested in Rivian’s factories. Rivian also owns equity in Mind Robotics and will be the first customer for its robots. Field said he is excited for the challenge in running the new startup. “Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time,” he said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.” Correction October 13th: Mind Robotics is a partner of Rivian, but not a spinoff. A previous version of this story misstated the relationship between the companies.

item.title: Rivian’s startup Mind Robotics hires former Ford EV chief Doug Field
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
Doug Field has worked on EVs at Ford and Tesla, the not-so-secret car project at Apple, and was employee No. 1 at Segway. Now the executive is turning his attention to Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s latest project: Mind Robotics. Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics, an industrial AI and robotics venture created last year by Scaringe and backed by Rivian. The news, shared onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 (taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco), is another sign that Mind Robotics is getting ready to scale up its early operations just one year after its founding. Scaringe will still be involved with Mind Robotics, but the day-to-day aspects of the business, including product, engineering, and operations, will be handled by Field. Mind Robotics, which has already amassed more than $1 billion in backing from Accel, Andreessen Horowitz, Eclipse, Kleiner Perkins, and the venture arms of Volkswagen and Salesforce, is building a full stack for industrial manufacturing. The purpose-built robots will run on foundation models with a goal of automating industrial and manufacturing tasks at scale. Rivian’s stake in Mind Robotics has been diluted since it took on additional backed; Rivian holds 32.1% ownership in Mind Robotics as of June 2026, per regulatory filings. Unlike the humanoid robots being developed by Tesla and others, Scaringe says Mind Robotics won’t attempt to mimic all the biomechanics of a human. The startup is also using Rivian as “a live, high-volume manufacturing environment for model training and deployment,” with Rivian being Mind Robotics’ first customer. Scaringe said on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday that he wanted someone like Field to help run Mind Robotics, and so he called him up to ask for a recommendation. “Him and I then really began digging into how important it is that we really think deeply and very intentionally about how we develop robotics and deploy robotics into our society, into our economy, and we found such alignment in how we thought about this from the overall mission of the business, but even more important, we found really deep alignment just in how we both work and how we build teams,” he said. Field left Ford in April after five years shaping the automaker’s electric vehicle and technology strategies. His departure was part of a wider reorganization of the automaker’s leadership. Prior to Ford, Field led Apple’s Project Titan, the electric, autonomous car project that was canceled in 2024. He also served as senior vice president of engineering at Tesla, where he oversaw development of the Model 3 and got the sedan through “production hell.” “Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important — and difficult — engineering challenges of our time,” Field said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.” Mind Robotics is the second company that Scaringe created outside of Rivian, following Also, a micromobility play that’s starting with high-end e-bikes. Like with Field and Mind Robotics, Scaringe is involved as chairman at Also but has tapped someone to run the day-to-day: Chris Yu, the former chief product officer of Specialized. Mind Robotics and Also operate as standalone companies, but Rivian has minority stakes in both. The company reported owning about a third of each startup as of June 30, 2026. This article has been updated to clarify that Rivian backs Mind Robotics, which was originally created by Rivian founder and CEO RJ Scaringe.

item.title: Gemini 4 Argon begins rolling out in Gemini app and Antigravity, but only if you pay
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica
Google revealed Gemini 4 Argon a few weeks ago, saying that it needed to move cautiously toward a full release because of the potential for nefarious use. Google seems to have worked all that out pretty quickly, though. Argon is beginning its wide rollout today, but it’s only coming to paying users at this time, and even those on lower-tier plans won’t have full access. Nothing about Gemini 4 Argon’s capabilities has changed. Google still points to the benchmarks it published late last month as evidence of the model’s advanced reasoning and agentic coding capabilities. The model is supposedly trained to refuse malicious instructions, and an automated misalignment monitor can stop processing if it detects an unintended workflow. Google claims Argon needs that because it’s so capable. The company has a few new examples of how Argon has helped inside Google, where it has been used by thousands of Googlers. Argon has reportedly been instrumental in making YouTube’s comment system more efficient. Argon identified redundant emoji rendering that, when eliminated, dropped server load by 45 percent. Engineers also turned Gemini 4 loose on the proprietary drone physics simulator used in Project Wing, and the AI found critical bugs that had been in the codebase since 2018. Google also notes that Argon has advanced its robotics program, showing a measurable step increase in embodied reasoning.

item.title: 5 clever ways Gemini can automate everyday tasks
item.description:
Source: Engadget
5 clever ways Gemini can automate everyday tasks Get the most out of Google's AI assistant. AI chatbots like Gemini have become quite popular for their ability to answer questions, but they can do much more than that. When it comes to Google's Gemini, you can also use it to schedule and automate tasks without having to handle them manually every time. For example, you can ask Gemini to check your calendar every day to calculate how much time you'll have between appointments, or even to constantly check for updates on a specific website. And if you pay for Google AI Pro or Ultra, Gemini Spark can reach into your inbox and calendar too. Once you've set up Gemini, here are a few things you can try first to automate your daily tasks. As mentioned in the example above, Gemini is great for helping you manage your daily commitments. Ask it to check your calendars every morning and give you an estimate of how much time you'll spend moving between each event. Try a prompt like, "Check my events for the day and estimate total travel and driving time using Maps every morning at 7:30AM." Of course, this will only work if you have all the relevant apps — like your calendar and email — connected to Gemini. Just be aware that Google may not take real-time traffic data into account, since it will use the data it has at the time the answer is generated. It's always a good idea to check the route on Maps before you leave. You can also ask Gemini to keep you up to date on a specific topic, like something you're personally interested in or monitoring for work. It can search the web at a set time and provide you with a summary of what it thinks is most important. A prompt like, "Every morning at 9AM, search for the latest news about Apple" is a good example. Google's own examples often feature daily and weekly summaries like this one. However, you can only run up to 10 scheduled actions at a time, so you might want to save them for important searches. You'll also receive a notification once your results are ready. If you like getting suggestions for things to do on the weekends, Gemini can help you with that, too. Ask it to suggest an itinerary with different places to have dinner every Friday and Saturday. Give it access to your location so it knows where you are and can search for nearby places without you even having to tell it. It's a great way to discover new cafes and restaurants every week. Try a prompt like, "Every Friday morning, plan my weekend with different ideas for cafes and restaurants to visit." Scheduled actions will not use your current location if you're traveling — it will use the location it accessed when you first set up the action. With Gemini, you can also define a set of instructions using skills, which are replacing Gems, to remember preferences across different conversations. Let's say you're working on a weekly newsletter and you need to follow institutional brand guidelines to ensure that the content aligns with the brand's communications. Just create a skill with all the instructions, and use the command to trigger that skill. Every time you use it, Gemini will apply the brand guidelines you've defined without you having to list them every time you want to generate your newsletter. Using skills is as simple as entering a command like "/skillname" in your Gemini chat. Google says that soon you'll use the @ symbol to invoke a skill instead of /. Gemini Spark is Google's always-on agent for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, and it keeps working even when your phone and laptop are off. For example, you can have Spark scan your entire week's worth of emails and summarize the most important ones. Not only that, but it can also create a to-do list and automatically add any appointments to your calendar. No need to waste time doing all of this manually. Just make sure to connect it to Gmail, Calendar and Drive first — they're all off by default. It's as simple as going into the settings and flipping a switch on. And don't worry, because Google says Spark is designed to check with you before taking any major actions, so it won't suddenly delete your important emails and files. One last thing: The availability of certain Gemini features may be limited to specific regions, so it's worth checking that as well.

item.title: Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July. Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI’s interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI’s first hardware device. These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components. The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited. The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services. In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data. Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations. U.S. District Judge Edward Davila didn’t greenlight all of Apple’s requests for expedited access to OpenAI documents and messages relevant to the case. But he did rule that Apple could access the interview materials, alongside private LINE messages (from a messaging app) between individuals named in the case, including OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng. The judge also approved depositions for Liu and Peng, along with a third individual, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer, Tang Yew Tan. All three are former Apple employees. However, the judge denied Apple’s request to expedite its access to OpenAI’s research and development in specific areas, like metal finishes and power management. He also denied several of Apple’s broader discovery requests, like access to OpenAI’s hardware research or information about what its former employees created while working at OpenAI. That denial isn’t final, though; the judge left the door open for Apple to narrow its requests and try again.

item.title: AI agents are coming to Rivian’s cars
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
Rivian recently rolled out an AI assistant that lets drivers and passengers interact with the company’s electric vehicles just by talking to them. But the carmaker’s founder and CEO, RJ Scaringe, said at TechCrunch Disrupt this week that, in the future, Rivian’s cars will be able to run AI agents made by other companies like Anthropic. “That’s where it becomes magical,” Scaringe said onstage. Scaringe didn’t say when Rivian would implement this, and the company declined to offer more details, pointing instead to the “AI & Autonomy Day” event it’s hosting in December. But it’s not hard to imagine how Rivian might integrate something like Claude, OpenAI’s Dots, or Meta’s Muse assistant into its software. The company has developed its in-car software from the ground up, instead of leaning on Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, and built a lot of its own applications, like navigation (though it has worked to integrate popular in-car apps like Apple Music). Rivian says it has created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle, and routes it to the right part of the car’s software. Most of the time, that involves what you’d expect: asking the car to turn down the temperature, activate the seat warmers, or summarize the news. “Think of it as like a traffic light. So if you ask the vehicle something, it decides what model it’s going to use. It can use a local model that’s running on the edge and the vehicle. If it’s a more complex question, it can go up to the cloud. And then even for that, we have different models that we use,” Scaringe said. As of May of this year, the agent could access external apps like Google Calendar. And Scaringe said at Disrupt the next step would be to add products from the frontier AI companies, though making them work in the car won’t be easy. “There’s a lot of plumbing behind the scenes we have to do to make sure that that works, and it’s not just within Rivian. That’s also a lot of coordination with the labs to make sure they enable that plumbing,” he said, adding that putting this kind of software near safety-critical systems means Rivian has to be extremely careful. “You wouldn’t want an agent to determine, ‘hey, it’s time to apply the brakes, or time to steer the vehicle.’ So anything that’s vehicle-level controls are not being handed to an agent,” he said. Instead, he thinks the implementation will look more like an extension of how people currently use these agentic apps. That would mean Rivian would have to find a way to connect the vehicle to all of the context that apps like Muse collect on their users. For example, Scaringe said, a driver could ask the Rivian assistant to turn on the ventilated seats before going deeper. “And then simultaneously say, ‘We were talking yesterday about this meal. I’m planning to have guests over on Friday. Can you help me think through what we’re going to make?’,” he said. The car could then pull the driver’s context from a conversation they had with the assistant on another device. Of course, Rivian wouldn’t be the first American car company to add AI agents to a car’s software. Earlier this year, Tesla added a feature that let users talk to both SpaceX’s Grok chatbot and also its Grok Bot assistant.

item.title: CedarDB wants one database to handle both transactions and analytics, as AI agents raise the stakes
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
Databases have traditionally been built for one of two jobs. Analytical databases help businesses spot trends and answer questions, while operational databases store the day-to-day records of transactions, like orders and payments. But the Munich-based database engine CedarDB supports both, and its approach has gained relevance with the rise of agentic AI, its co-founder and CEO Moritz Sichert told TechCrunch. CedarDB has been in the making for the last decade, but its current momentum stems from enterprise companies whose existing data stacks may have been well suited to storing years of transactions, yet less suited to quickly answering analytical questions asked in natural language about that data. CedarDB’s questioning of the divide between analytical and operational queries is a by-product of its focus on efficiency. The company is a Technical University of Munich spinout based on Umbra, a research project that was built from scratch to beat legacy database engines at processing speed by making the most of modern hardware. With five Umbra researchers as its co-founders, CedarDB kept that approach, promising faster performance without requiring more CPUs or processing power and memory — and requiring few changes from customers. In particular, its team made sure CedarDB was compatible with PostgreSQL, an open source database system. According to Sichert, this compatibility with the popular database helps keep switching costs low, since users don’t need to rebuild their apps. It also has an added advantage: CedarDB follows the logic LLMs are most familiar with as a result of their training. That decision is one of many choices that proved lucky in retrospect, Sichert said. But it wasn’t all luck. In a blog post, co-founder Christian Winter detailed key priorities the team set after leaving academia, “such as reliability, fault tolerance and compatibility with popular tools.” Not all of the answers were obvious. The team strongly debated whether it should launch a cloud offering right away. In the end, it launched CedarDB Enterprise as an on-premise offering alongside its free version, CedarDB Community Edition, both announced in May of last year at the same time as it announced a €5.3 million seed funding round (approximately $6 million). The cloud offering was only delayed, though, not abandoned. After conducting beta testing with users who had signed up for its waitlist, the company on Wednesday announced limited availability of CedarDB Cloud onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, where it’s competing with 20 other startups vying to win TechCrunch’s prestigious Startup Battlefield competition. A fully managed, cloud-hosted version will likely help CedarDB expand its user base beyond large enterprises. It will also make it better prepared to compete with the likes of Databricks, a major data company that seems to have reached the same conclusion as the German startup. At its Data + AI Summit in June, the American company cited “the agentic era” as the reason why it was launching LTAP, a new data architecture aiming to “[unify] transactions, analytics, streaming, and operational data on a single copy of storage in the lake.” It is too early to tell how disruptive this might be, but Sichert interprets Databricks’ move as another sign that there is demand for what CedarDB does. The startup plans to serve its first cloud users with its current team of 14 people, but Sichert expects it will need a larger team once it gets more traction. “And this is where we would raise our next round.” Pictured from left to right: CedarDB founders Moritz Sichert, Lukas Vogel, Philipp Fent, Dominik Durner, and Christian Winter.

item.title: Researchers warn ChatGPT for Teens poses serious risks
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
- Researchers tested ChatGPT for Teens with more than 4,000 prompts - They found significant gaps in its safety protections and safeguards - ChatGPT failed to trigger parental alerts during some serious mental health conversations OpenAI's efforts to make ChatGPT safer for teenagers have run into an uncomfortable problem. A new investigation suggests that many of the protections designed to reassure parents aren't working particularly well, even when the chatbot is dealing with potentially dangerous conversations. After putting ChatGPT through more than 4,000 prompts, researchers concluded that the company's teen-focused experience poses an unacceptable risk to young users. The study from Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute examined ChatGPT before and after OpenAI introduced ChatGPT for Teens on August 18. The researchers used accounts registered to teenagers aged 13 to 17 and consulted medical experts, including child psychiatrists and a pediatrician, to evaluate its responses. Their findings were troubling enough that the organization recommended OpenAI restrict ChatGPT to adults until the problems are resolved. ChatGPT for Teens was supposed to make the popular chatbot a more appropriate companion for younger users, with additional protections against harmful content, parental notifications, and features encouraging learning rather than simply handing over homework answers. OpenAI also promised to discourage overly personal relationships with the chatbot and help teenagers maintain healthier boundaries with AI. The new report suggests there is still a considerable gap between those ambitions and what happens when teenagers actually use it. ChatGPT's parental notifications are intended to alert caregivers when a teenager may be experiencing serious distress. So researchers spent up to an hour discussing suicidal thoughts, self-harm, and disordered eating through newly created accounts linked to parents. According to the report, none of those conversations triggered a parental notification, although the researchers eventually generated alerts using older accounts with weeks of relevant conversation history. ChatGPT is also supposed to direct teenagers to appropriate help during mental health emergencies, but the study found that ChatGPT failed to do so in more than 25% of situations experts designed to require it. There were some successes, including ChatGPT's refusal to engage in explicit sexual roleplay. However, the researchers also found that the chatbot continued responding in ways that suggested it had feelings, preferences, and moods, despite OpenAI's efforts to discourage teenagers from treating it like a human friend. That matters when younger users may already be inclined to confide in an endlessly patient chatbot that never seems too busy to listen. The problems extended beyond serious safety concerns into some of ChatGPT's everyday educational features. OpenAI's Study mode is designed to guide students through problems using explanations, hints, and questions rather than immediately providing answers. Researchers discovered that teenagers could sometimes bypass that approach by selecting a "Show me the answer" option, allowing ChatGPT to complete assignments instead. The Study Hours feature, designed for parents to help encourage educational use, also failed to stop workarounds. Simply removing the @study prefix from a prompt could make ChatGPT go back to normal. And the AI didn't remind users to take breaks nearly as often as it should. The study also found problems with the much-touted age detection system created by OpenAI to identify younger users and automatically apply appropriate protections. Repeatedly saying they were 13 didn't prompt ChatGPT to move the test accounts from the adult experience. The larger issue is that ChatGPT is becoming a regular part of teenagers' lives. While helping with schoolwork and answering personal questions is great, having teenage users demands considerably more reliable safeguards than a typical productivity app for adults. We offered OpenAI the opportunity to comment on the survey, but haven't received a response so far. We'll update the story if we do. item.title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review
When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.” Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined. Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code. That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data, including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use. There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker, this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales. While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left. Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore. Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. AI’s recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems. Don’t be fooled by this summer of AI hype Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. item.title: OpenAI says it found a 'sophisticated recording device' hidden in its offices
item.description:
Source: Engadget
OpenAI says it found a 'sophisticated recording device' hidden in its offices Of course, it asked AI what to do about it. US federal prosecutors have arrested and charged a Saudi national with allegedly hiding a sophisticated recording device inside of OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters. Per the San Francisco Standard, Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer who had been with the company since July 2025, has been accused of attempting to record oral conversations between OpenAI employees. Alfozan allegedly left a DIY recording device inside of an executive conference room he wasn't authorized to enter or use. We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we're... — OpenAI Newsroom (@OpenAINewsroom) October 13, 2026 According to the complaint the San Francisco Standard saw, prosecutors said meetings inside the room often involved confidential information, including details related to the company's product roadmap, research and government engagement. OpenAI found the device on September 30 plugged into a USB port on the back of a TV. Alfozan appears to have used toilet paper to conceal the device. According to prosecutors, he used a "productivity tool" to collect information about OpenAI's facilities. He may have also used a chatbot to ask how to build, install and hide a remote recording device. On a chatbot account tied to his spouse, investigators allegedly found prompts asking the AI model how to "build a continuous audio recorder" and "encrypt the SD card." In a statement published to X, OpenAI says it used its own AI models to "understand the device," which it also called sophisticated. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated," OpenAI wrote in the post. OpenAI did not immediately respond to Engadget's request for comment and more information. OpenAI determined the device was installed sometime in and around September 28. On October 5, Alfozan allegedly left behind a bag somewhere else in OpenAI's office. The company's security personnel found Alfozan's wallet, ID and a second recording device inside the bag. Alfozan made his first court appearance on Tuesday. If convicted, he faces up to five years in a federal prison, a $250,000 fine and three years of supervised release.

item.title: Martin Shkreli livestreamed himself violating lifetime pharma ban, FTC says
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica
Martin Shkreli—the ex-pharmaceutical executive infamous for illegally hiking the price of a lifesaving anti-parasitic drug by more than 4,000 percent and getting a seven-year prison sentence for the fraudulent scheme he used to do it—has been under a lifetime ban from the pharmaceutical industry since 2022. However, according to the Federal Trade Commission and the attorneys general of seven states, Shkreli has “flagrantly and repeatedly” violated that ban nearly the entire time—allegedly by trading stock in dozens of drug companies and discussing the industry during livestreams on social media. On Tuesday, the FTC and the seven states asked a federal judge to hold Shkreli in contempt for the alleged violations. The states include New York, California, Illinois, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Virginia—the same states that joined the FTC in suing Shkreli in 2020 over the “elaborate anticompetitive scheme” involving the anti-parasitic drug, Daraprim. The scheme raised the price from $17.50 per pill to $750 per pill virtually overnight, while blocking generic competitors from entering the market. In 2022, the federal court recognized the “seriousness” of issuing such a lifetime industry ban, but ruled that “Shkreli’s egregious, deliberate, repetitive, long-running, and ultimately dangerous illegal conduct warrants imposition of an injunction of this scope.” The ban, among many things, “explicitly prohibits” Shkreli from owning stock in pharmaceutical companies and making public statements that could influence a pharmaceutical company’s business, according to the FTC and the states. With the alleged violations, the FTC and the states are now seeking to force Shkreli to divest from all pharmaceutical companies and pay a fine equal to his profits from trading pharmaceutical company stocks. They also want the court to lay out “clear and escalating consequences” if Shkreli violates the ban in the future, including further financial penalties and incarceration.

item.title: ESA targets Anbernic emulation handhelds as "superfake" piracy enablers
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica
For years, Chinese hardware manufacturers have carved out a market niche with an array of handheld Android gaming devices focused on retro emulation and/or more modern game-streaming capabilities. Now, though, a major game industry trade group is targeting one of those manufacturers, Anbernic, asking the US Trade Representative (USTR) to add the company to its list of “Notorious Markets” that “engage in or facilitate substantial copyright piracy or trademark counterfeiting.” TorrentFreak was among the first to notice the request from the Entertainment Software Association (ESA), which was submitted to the USTR last week. In it, the US trade group—which represents major publishers including Nintendo, Microsoft, PlayStation, Amazon, Epic, EA, Ubisoft, and more—notes that Anbernic devices “are routinely offered or shipped with removable memory cards preloaded with hundreds or thousands of unauthorized copies of copyright-protected video games published by ESA members.” While many online sellers do include an SD card full of ROMs alongside emulation hardware of all types, Anbernic itself does not appear to do the same when selling directly from its website. Regardless, the ESA argues that these ROM-laden Anbernic devices selling through “normal retail channels” help to “normalize hardware-based piracy by delivering illicit catalogues through a polished consumer product.” This, the ESA says, meets the threshold for a “superfake,” an ill-defined designation that applies to “high-quality counterfeit trademark goods … on a commercial scale.” Being included on the USTR’s Notorious Market List wouldn’t bring any additional direct legal consequences for a company like Anbernic. However, the USTR says the list “encourages the responsible authorities to step up efforts to combat piracy and counterfeiting” and notes that the list itself “increase[s] public awareness and help market operators and governments prioritize intellectual property enforcement efforts that protect American businesses and their workers.” Inclusion on the list could also presage a Section 301 investigation that could lead to legal consequences or restrictive import controls on the devices.

item.title: Topgolf saved over $11.3 million after leaving VMware
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica
Topgolf’s VMware costs were going to increase by 400 percent under Broadcom. To avoid that cost, the sports entertainment company moved 12,000 virtual machines (VMs) to VergeIO’s VergeOS and has saved over $11 million so far. Before migrating, Topgolf’s VMware connection “ran very deep,” Scott Forehand, Topgolf’s global infrastructure manager, told Ars Technica. Topgolf has over 100 locations worldwide featuring interactive golf games with real-time shot tracking and digital analytics. The company used vSphere and ESXi for decades and started using VxRail, the hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) platform that VMware co-engineered with Dell, in 2017. Topgolf employees previously participated in numerous VMware customer councils and have been interviewed for books on how Topgolf used vSphere and Horizon (now Omnissa Horizon), per Forehand, who is a leader of the Dallas/Ft. Worth VMware User Group. But Broadcom’s decision to stop selling VMware perpetual licenses and bundle VMware products into fewer, larger, and more expensive SKUs led Topgolf, as well as many other VMware customers, to look elsewhere. With VMware’s strategic changes complicating future planning, Topgolf decided to migrate its on-premises workloads, including those for its venues, offices, labs, and data centers. Twenty Topgolf venues are still running VxRail with the VMware Cloud Foundation software stack. Forehand expects Topgolf to be completely off VMware by the second week of December. He added: Overall, we reduced or eliminated over $11.3 [million] in combined infrastructure costs prior to the adjustments in hardware cost in the market. Comparatively, it’s much more now when you look at the cost of a solution similar to the configuration of the old VxRail solution we installed. The money Topgolf saved by moving to VergeIO isn’t typical because Topgolf has larger needs than many organizations. However, saving money on software licensing and avoiding proprietary HCI appliances and separate tools for data protection, replication, and multi-site management is common for VergeOS users coming from VMware, VergeIO Chief Marketing Officer George Crump told Ars. “Most customers who move from VMware see meaningful reductions in all three,” he said.
