item.title: The USB flash drive feels like the most obvious invention in computing. Its messy origin story says otherwise
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
It is easy to look at a small plastic drive on a desk and assume someone sat down, drew a blueprint, and built it out of thin air. Plenty of devices were genius inventions that one person could lay claim to, sometimes building off the foundation of others. However, hardware history rarely works like that, and combining parts from separate inventions usually turns into a brawl over who crossed the finish line first. The USB flash drive is no different. Older parts came together to push out the floppy disk Way before any USB flash drive showed up on store shelves, the key tech you'd need to build one was already getting used all over the computer world. By the late 1990s, putting these parts together into a thumb-sized storage gadget was just the next logical step. It didn't come out of nowhere. If you look at how the dominoes fell, it was bound to happen eventually. The solid-state base was laid down at Toshiba Corporation back in the 1980s under Dr. Fujio Masuoka. In 1980, Masuoka had the idea of non-volatile floating-gate semiconductor memory, which Toshiba showed off at the 1984 IEEE International Electron Devices Meeting as NOR flash memory. NOR flash let you do byte-level random access, so it was awesome for running system firmware, but its design needed individual contact vias for every memory cell, which jacked up manufacturing costs and gave you lousy storage density. To dodge these physical roadblocks, Masuoka and his crew rolled out the NAND flash architecture at the 1987 IEDM. By stringing floating-gate MOSFET cells together in series instead of parallel arrays, NAND flash got rid of most of those direct contact vias. That shrank each cell to about 60% of the space a NOR cell took up. To make NAND flash into a solid mass storage medium, Toshiba engineers Riichiro Shirota and Koji Sakui tweaked the programming mechanics in the late 80s. In 1991, Toshiba released the first commercial four-megabit NAND flash chip. Around the same time, the USB standard was emerging, with Intel engineer Ajay Bhatt playing a major role in its development before it officially launched in 1996. USB 1.0 brought a couple of features that turned out to be huge. One of the big ones was hot-plugging, which let users hook up or yank devices without rebooting. Another was five-volt power sent right through the cable, so you didn't need external batteries or power bricks. The USB Implementers Forum also set up the USB Mass Storage Class protocol, using the Bulk-Only Transport profile. This standardized software interface lets host operating systems spot and manage external block storage without needing custom drivers. This combination pretty much killed the floppy disk. By the late 1990s, floppies still dedicated drive bays inside computers. I spent a lot of my childhood and early teens using floppy disks; I miss them. However, USBs are far better; they just don't feel the same. Different groups tried to make the hardware Companies across the globe filed claims at the same time Figuring out who invented the USB flash drive is incredibly messy because it feels like it happened all at once in different places. Between 1998 and 2001, patent filings, internal memos, product launches, and factory milestones piled up across several continents. Because different parties hit different milestones, figuring out who deserves credit depends a lot on what you're making and where. In April 1999, Israeli storage firm M-Systems, led by Amir Ban, Dov Moran, and Oron Ogdan, filed a patent application in the United States. That gave them the first formal legal claim. Their filing described a PC flash disk using a USB interface, non-volatile flash memory, and a custom controller ASIC. In September 1999, IBM engineer Shimon Shmueli wrote up an internal idea at IBM for a USB flash drive that could replace the floppy drive in ThinkPad laptops. His write-up described a removable solid-state memory module with a built-in USB connector, but IBM never got a patent on the core design. M-Systems started selling it as the DiskOnKey in late 2000 and made a deal with IBM, which sold the same hardware worldwide as the IBM USB Memory Key. Months after M-Systems' U.S. filing, Chinese engineers Deng Guoshun and Cheng Xiaohua of Netac Technology filed a patent application in China for an electronic flash memory external storage method and device. Netac's patent was granted in China in 2002, and U.S. patents came later. Those patents became the legal backbone for its product, the OnlyDisk. Singapore-based Trek 2000 International, led by CEO Henn Tan, was the first to show one off in public and get it into stores. After filing a priority patent in Singapore in February 2000, Trek publicly launched its ThumbDrive at the CeBIT trade show in Hanover, Germany, and it hit stores soon after. Then in November 2000, Malaysian engineer Pua Khein-Seng co-founded Phison Electronics Corporation in Taiwan. In 2001, Phison pulled off a big win by designing the first single-chip USB flash drive controller. Phison's System-on-a-Chip puts the USB physical layer transceiver, memory management unit, and flash controller all on a single piece of silicon. That brought costs way down and made it possible to crank these out all over the world. This is all really hard to keep up with and has caused so many issues. The legal record will never give us one clear winner Local patent laws split the credit across different borders Unfortunately, all these things happened at around the same time, and we don't know at what point it truly became the USB flash drive. None of them started as the USB drive we know today, which is why there are so many disagreements. The thing is, all of these pieces ended up in the USB drive, so the waters are really muddy. There's no one inventor everyone agrees on, because courts and patent offices in different countries use different rules for the same timeline. Patents only count in the country that grants them, so who gets credit changes depending on where you live. It doesn't matter who did it; it matters that technology moved forward Looking for one person to pin a medal on usually misses how manufacturing works. There's no tidy story with one hero here, and the legal records are still a mess today. Honestly, how these things made it onto store shelves is the more interesting part. Somebody had to get them out the door while everyone else argued over who thought of it first.

item.title: Your SSD has a tiny computer inside, and it’s doing more than just saving files
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
SSDs are more than just flash memory chips soldered to a PCB. They’re still relatively simple designs, but they can’t function without a small chip next to the flash that manages how and where data is written, moved, and erased, along with a plethora of other responsibilities. And the controller really is a tiny computer Both hard drives and flash memory-based storage media, including SSDs, have a small chip inside called a controller. The controller is the most important part of every SSD because without it, the SSD in your PC wouldn’t work. In fact, if the flash memory chips on it work flawlessly but the controller gives out, the drive is dead in the water. dedicated hardware for tasks like error correction and encryption. SSD controllers also run their own firmware, which is just as important for the SSD’s performance as the controller’s hardware. Think of the firmware as a tiny OS for the controller; it can even get updates that improve performance and fix bugs. Each controller also needs memory to work, mostly for the mapping table that tracks where data is stored on the flash chips. The mapping table is saved in the flash memory, but many SSDs keep a copy of it in a DRAM chip, so the controller can access it quickly. Cheaper DRAM-less SSDs instead keep part of it in a small slice of your PC’s RAM, thanks to a feature called Host Memory Buffer (HMB). Naturally, not every controller is equally good at its job. The best ones pair with flagship SSDs, while more affordable drives use less capable controllers. That is why you can have two SSDs with the same NAND flash, with one faster than the other simply because it has a better controller. So if you’re in the market for a new SSD, don’t just focus on the PCIe generation and the speeds on the box. Also, check which controller powers it. The controller is responsible for writing and fetching data to and from the flash memory Think of it as a parking lot manager for your data If you imagine the flash memory on an SSD as a parking lot, the controller is the parking lot manager, telling drivers where to park and where to find their cars later. Depending on how well and how fast the manager does their job, drivers find a parking space, or their car, faster or slower. For instance, when you download a file to your PC from the web, all the bytes of data that make up the file arrive at the SSD’s controller before it writes them to flash memory. As they come through the gate, the controller checks the mapping table, which tracks the flash memory down to blocks (usually several megabytes) and pages (usually 16KB). It then finds free pages and directs the data to them. On the other hand, when you open a file, the operating system asks the SSD for it, and the controller looks up the mapping table, finds where the file's parts are stored, reads them from the flash memory, and sends them back to the operating system. The faster the controller does its job, the faster the SSD is, as long as the flash memory can keep up. The quickest consumer controllers are found in PCIe 5.0 SSDs, helping them hit breakneck sequential speeds that can surpass 14GB/s, but only if the drive on the other end of the transfer is just as fast. Most workloads, though, will see the SSD run at much lower speeds, since the other side usually caps it, whether that’s another SSD or your internet plan. But controllers do much more than just move data in and out of the flash memory. They’re actually working around the clock as long as your computer is turned on, managing all kinds of stuff. SSD controllers juggle a ton of other tasks as well Huge responsibility coupled with intense workloads Even when you’re doing nothing on your computer, several background processes constantly access the boot drive. Every time they do, they go through the controller, which has the back-breaking job of constantly reading and writing data to the flash chips. But the controller is busy as a bee even on an SSD used only for storage and sitting idle. For instance, it handles garbage collection and TRIM operations. Since flash memory can only be erased in whole blocks, garbage collection moves needed data from a block to new pages, then erases the whole block so it can be reused. TRIM, on the other hand, tells the SSD which pages hold deleted data, so the controller doesn’t waste time moving them during garbage collection. Another key role of the controller is managing bad blocks, which can be faulty from the factory or wear out over time. It does this through over-provisioning: a bit of extra space on every SSD that only the controller can access. The controller uses this space to replace bad blocks with fresh ones, as well as for garbage collection and wear leveling. Wear leveling is needed because each NAND cell can only handle a limited number of write and erase cycles before it wears out and becomes unusable. The controller spreads writes evenly across the drive so all cells wear out at the same rate and no part of the SSD dies prematurely. The controller also monitors the drive’s overall health, manages power consumption, and slows down if it or the flash chips get too hot (thermal throttling). On many SSDs, it encrypts the data written to the NAND as well. On top of that, it scrambles the data before writing it so 0s and 1s are evenly spread across the pages, which helps keep data intact. And that’s not all. SSD controllers also have to perform error correction, without which NAND flash would be pretty much unusable. They also handle data refresh, rewriting data to new pages before small changes in the NAND cells’ charge cause errors to pile up and make the data unreadable. Last but not least, most SSDs use part of their flash as a fast SLC cache, and the controller manages it by writing incoming data there first and moving it to its final spot later, usually when the drive is idle. SSD controllers are more complex than meets the eye As you can see, the controller’s roles are extensive, so it’s no surprise it’s, hands down, the most complex component of every SSD. You wouldn’t be wrong to call it a tiny computer, because that’s really what it is, only instead of Windows or macOS, it runs firmware that lets it do its job and communicate with your computer's operating system. So the next time you’re shopping for an SSD, remember that the tiny chip doing all this work matters as much as, if not more than, the flash memory it manages.

item.title: This ESP32 project gave my office a "mood ring" that reacts to calendar events, the weather, and more
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
My kids bought mood rings in the summer that change color, supposedly to reflect your current mood. This gave me an idea for building a mood ring of my own for my office that would give me useful information at a glance. I gave my Cheap Yellow Display another job I wanted something different from a typical dashboard A Cheap Yellow Display (CYD) is a very versatile tool for the price. It's an ESP32 board with a small, built-in touchscreen display, and you can buy one for around $15. With ESPHome, you can create configuration files that compile into firmware for the CYD, letting it do whatever you want. I have a CYD in my home office that I use as part of my music discovery setup. A playlist of new music is generated each week, and when it plays, the album artwork is displayed on the CYD. I can tap the screen to add songs to a separate shortlist playlist, and when I play through this shortlist, tapping the screen automatically adds the album to my Apple Music library. I wanted a good way to use the CYD when I wasn't playing music, and sharing information seemed like a good option. I didn't just want a boring dashboard, so I decided to get a little more experimental. The idea was to have the CYD display a mood ring that would change based on current and upcoming events. The first thing that I wanted to display was the weather. I use the OpenWeatherMap integration in Home Assistant to provide details of the weather conditions in my location. It exposes conditions such as sunny, partly cloudy, rain, fog, and more. The mood ring doesn't cover every condition, but it displays strong yellows for sunny weather, softer yellow for partly cloudy conditions, blue patches for rain, and muted blue-gray patches for cloud and fog. As the weather changes, so does the mood ring, so I can see the current conditions at a glance. There's also a simplified text label describing the weather condition, such as SUN, SUN/CLOUD, and RAIN. If I'm playing music in the office, the weather colors still remain, but the mood ring dances a little, causing the patterns to shift. It doesn't analyze the audio or match the beat, and it doesn't really serve any purpose other than to make the mood ring feel a little more alive. My calendar events change the ring's mood The ring changes the closer the event gets Perhaps the most useful part of the mood ring is that it can give me a visual indication of how close upcoming events are. An hour before the next event is due to start, the ring shows a small patch of red. This red arc expands further around the ring as the event gets nearer and then pulses during the final five minutes before the event is due. Text in the center of the mood ring shows a countdown to the event so I can see how long is left in minutes. The event name appears at the bottom of the screen, so I can see at a glance what event is upcoming and how long I have before it starts. The events come from a calendar within Home Assistant, which pulls together key events from my work calendar as well as our family calendar. The CYD uses these events' start times to know when to start displaying the red portions of the ring. The red arc never expands to the full circumference of the mood ring, topping out at 85% of the circle. That way, I can still see the weather colors even when an event is almost due. The final thing that the mood ring does is show me when I've been sitting down for too long. I have an mmWave presence sensor in my home office, with a zone set up that only covers my office chair. The sensor can tell with good accuracy when I'm sitting at my desk and when I'm not. After 30 minutes, the ring begins to fade. By 60 minutes, the ring looks increasingly frazzled, and by 90 minutes it becomes dark purple with jagged red edges. If I leave my chair for five minutes, the ring resets to its original appearance. The time I've been sitting also appears in the middle of the ring, so I can see exactly how long it's been, though an event countdown replaces it if an event is coming up. The ring becomes a visualization of what I'm doing to my body by sitting still for too long. It's a useful visual reminder that encourages me to get up and move around more often. I've never been a big fan of smart home dashboards; for me, a smart home should require as little manual control as possible, with most things happening automatically. Some information is always useful to see, but a mood ring is far more interesting than another display with buttons and numbers.

item.title: Amazon and Google finally have real competition in the smart home
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
Amazon and Google have largely had the smart home world to themselves, at least for those who aren't interested in a solution like Home Assistant. They've not only built a load of hardware, but they also created whole ecosystems with tens of thousands of supported devices between them. They're not without their flaws, but they generally offer a turnkey smart home experience. Apple's strategy, meanwhile, has been marred by an inconsistent lineup and a convoluted Apple Home device approval process. But now the Apple HomeView, the Home Collection, and the company's embrace of Thread and Matter show that Apple is getting serious about the smart home. While there are still problems, Amazon and Google have real cause to be worried. Amazon and Google are both old hands at smart displays, having released their first models several years ago. However, Apple's belated entry into the space with the HomeView is meaningful in itself. It's finally giving people a major alternative to screens like the Echo Show and Nest Hub. You'll need to be deep in Apple's universe for this to make the most sense (though services like Spotify will work), but many Alexa and Google Home users are already iPhone owners. And there are a few areas where Apple pulls ahead despite mostly playing catch-up. The option to move music between devices just by putting your iPhone in front of the HomeView's display is convenient, I'd love to transfer the music from my car to a smart display effortlessly. It can turn web recipes into step-by-step instructions, and show nine live camera feeds at once. And yes, that iMac G4-like design is arguably more attractive than what Amazon or Google has to offer. It's true that Amazon and Google do some things better. They're not tied to a single ecosystem, work with a wider range of services, and still have more devices to choose from. You can get larger screens, physical privacy shutters, and even models that double as kitchen TVs. But the HomeView is a strong start and goes a long way toward making Apple Home relevant. Apple has never had equivalents to Amazon's Ring or Google's Nest smart home accessories. You've had to go searching, even for basics like security cameras. Why bother when Apple's competitors are one-stop shops? The introduction of the Apple Home Collection upends that expectation. LG and Schneider Electric might have co-designed the line, but the impact is the same: you can buy a wide selection of accessories that are optimized for Apple Home, including single-tap pairing and full Siri control. While there's still the need for some third-party gear (lighting, for example), I'd be much more confident buying a HomeView or HomePod knowing the most essential categories are covered. That whole-home approach might make it harder for Apple Home allies like Ecobee to stand out. But I'm hoping that the Home Collection will inspire better products. It certainly reduces the appeal of Amazon and Google, if just for iPhone fans who'd rather not go through comparison shopping or fussy setup rituals to get going. The higher-than-usual prices of the Home Collection will let at least some manufacturers carve out niches for themselves. If there's a more pressing worry, it's that the Apple Home ecosystem might not grow larger, no matter how well-designed the accessories might be. Amazon and Google have momentum on their side, and that's difficult to stop despite Apple's size. The Home Collection could be necessary to guarantee at least some accessory choices. Amazon and Google have faced their share of privacy uproars. Amazon's track record is rough between Ring's police collaboration and concerns about possible mass surveillance. Google, meanwhile, is dealing with multiple lawsuits over allegations it collects strangers' face data without consent. As much as the accusations of spying are sometimes overblown, the history doesn't exactly inspire much confidence. Apple maintains that privacy is at the heart of the HomeView and its other new smart home devices. Camera and mic data is kept locally and separately. You need a paired iPhone or iPad to access your personal data on the HomeView. Facial recognition is present, but Apple maintains that data is completely encrypted (including for the Home Collection), and that cloud-stored video is inaccessible to anyone for the 10 days it remains online. Even the indoor camera tilts down when you get home. This doesn't mean you should blindly trust Apple. I'd like security experts to test Apple's claims, and LG has drawn flak for purportedly eavesdropping on TV users and installing adware through monitors. But Apple has long put a greater emphasis on privacy than its challengers, and says that extends to the LG and Schneider devices. That trustworthiness could easily lure would-be buyers away from Amazon and Google.

item.title: I stopped scrolling endlessly and started watching better movies with these 5 streaming challenges
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
Everyone has found themselves scrolling through all their streaming services for ages, struggling to find something interesting to watch. Sometimes, though, it isn't the streaming service that is the problem. Sometimes we avoid watching good content simply because we aren't willing to take a chance on something new. There are tons to watch if you're willing to stick your toe outside your comfort zone. In my eyes, everyone is guilty, including myself. I find that the best way to push myself to discover something new is to impose mini-challenges on myself. I stick to a set of rules for a week and only watch movies and shows that fit my criteria. Whether watching stuff from one genre or exploring the filmography of directors and actors, I've always walked away with new titles to add to my list of favorites. Content you haven't watched with themes you love One of the easiest rules that I impose on myself is one where I pick a genre that I like and stick to it. This means that I can choose things that follow the same overarching themes and trends that I know I already like, but I can avoid things that I've already watched in that genre, exposing myself to all sorts of stuff that I haven't watched before. Most recently, I stuck to science fiction for a week. It's one of my favorite genres, with the Star Wars and Alien franchises being such impactful and defining content throughout my childhood (and adulthood). I've watched a lot of sci-fi content in my life, but there was so much more that I discovered through this challenge. Some of the content didn't quite hit the mark, but I watched things like Ex Machina, Minority Report, and Coherence for the first time, all of which I loved. Pick a director you like, and work through their filmography While a small group of directors are capable of churning out nothing but hits, most have their fair share of box office flops alongside their successes. Just because a movie or show doesn't become popular, however, doesn't mean it isn't worth watching. With the sheer volume of content out there, we sometimes miss some of these hidden gems. Picking a director and watching your way through their work can open your eyes to content you otherwise never would have watched. It's something that I have done since I was a teenager, starting with the greats like Tarantino, Kubrick, and Scorsese. After recently watching Dune, I decided to watch Denis Villeneuve's movies. I rewatched things I loved, like Blade Runner 2049 and Arrival, but I was surprised by some films I hadn't really heard of before, with Incendies being my personal favorite. Follow the career of an actor from start to finish The best performances aren't always blockbusters Actors can elevate movies and shows to another level. A mediocre script or uninspired idea gets overshadowed by the performance of an actor. Sometimes, without an actor and their brilliant performance, the films they star in wouldn't be nearly as successful. One of the most obvious examples is Castaway, with Tom Hanks being the core that held everything together. This entry isn't one that I go back to all the time, but rather when I am particularly impressed with an actor's portrayal in something I'm watching. An example is after I watched Joker, with Joaquin Phoenix blowing me away with his rendition of Arthur Fleck. This was how I discovered one of my all-time favorite movies, Her, a story about a man falling in love with an AI, with Pheonix playing the lead of Theodore. Watch the best movies and series from a specific decade It's pretty easy to get sucked into only watching the latest releases. We like to stick to what we know, and sometimes it's easier to only watch stuff that is familiar. If you don't step outside your comfort zone, though, you'll miss a lot of great content. Picking a decade and watching some of the most iconic bits of film and television can broaden your perspective in so many ways. I do this often, and with such a huge pool of content out there, I often revisit decades, watching new stuff every time. I recently went back to the 90s, finally catching up on some classics that I definitely should have already watched. As a movie enthusiast, it's a bit embarrassing to admit, but I watched Fargo for the first time only a couple of weeks ago. Don't overlook content just because it's animated Animation can capture magic that isn't otherwise possible I have always been a champion of animated movies and series. There is a tendency to think that just because something is animated means that it is created exclusively for children and isn't capable of capturing the same depth that you get with live-action content. Animation is such a vibrant medium and has been used to tell some of the most impactful and emotional stories. It's a medium that you definitely shouldn't be scared to explore. I love embarking on animation-only weeks. I get to revisit classics that have a special place in my heart, such as The Iron Giant and Howl's Moving Castle. I also always get to discover new shows and movies. The last time I did an animation week, I added a bunch of stuff to my list of favorites, including Cyberpunk: Edgerunners, Princess Mononoke, and Your Name. Broaden your horizons and challenge your usual habits We're in an era where movies and shows are more accessible. With the wide selection of streaming services that we subscribe to, just about everything is available at the push of a button. In this vast world of content, you're missing out if you don't try new things. The above challenges have always helped me take that step into the unknown, and I've always felt a little enlightened after the fact.

item.title: How to connect a Googlebook to a printer
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
Need to print a document from your Googlebook? Thankfully, the process of connecting to a printer takes less than a minute, and although most Googlebook apps lack any printing functionality, Chrome and other standard Google tools will let you print a page or document with a simple keyboard shortcut. Use the Ctrl + P shortcut or print from the three-dot menu This process works over both Wi-Fi and USB Printer discovery on the Googlebook is fairly seamless. Connect your printer to the Googlebook over USB, or connect both devices to the same Wi-Fi network, and your printer will appear as an option in the print menu. To access the print menu, open a web page or document and press the Ctrl + P keys on your Googlebook. Alternatively, go into the three-dot menu at the top-right corner of your browser and select the "Print" option. Now, navigate to the top-left corner of the print menu and press the "Select a printer" button. Select your printer, determine your paper size, color settings, paper orientation, and other options, then hit the large "Print" button in the bottom-right corner of the window. Most Google-made apps, including Google Photos, follow this schema—you can print using Ctrl + P or by selecting "Print" from the three-dot menu. Third-party apps may offer printing functionality through their "Share" menu (the icon that looks like three dots connected together with lines). That said, the vast majority of apps on Googlebook are simply Android mobile apps and do not provide any built-in printing functionality at this time. Using Bluetooth? Try the printer's Android app This may also help when Wi-Fi or USB printing fails Bluetooth printers typically require a manufacturer app, just as they do on Android. Thankfully, Googlebook has a built-in process for installing these apps. Open your Settings, click the "Connected Devices" tab in the sidebar, select the "Connection preferences" button that pops up, and click "Printing." Then, tap "Add service," and a Google Play window will appear onscreen. Select and install the app that matches your Bluetooth printer's branding. You can also get to your printer settings by typing "Printer" in the Settings app's search bar. Some options on the Play Store are designed for universal printer connectivity—you should select one of these if your printer's manufacturer app isn't available. Alternatively, you can check the manufacturer's website for an APK file. If an APK file is available, download it to your Googlebook and double-click it to kick off the installation process. How to diagnose printing errors on a Googlebook Check your notifications or go to Printer Settings It's almost impossible to use a printer without running into errors. And, like Windows or macOS, GooglebookOS doesn't always make printing errors easy to find. There are two ways to read printing errors on your Googlebook. The fastest option is to simply pull down your notification menu, which you can access by clicking the bell icon in the top-right corner of your screen (or by swiping down from the top-right corner of the touchscreen). But the notification tray can be a bit messy. If you need a cleaner, more detailed view, you'll need to go into your Printer Settings. Open your Googlebook's Settings app, select "Connected Devices," and tap the "Connection preferences" button. Then, select "Printing," and you'll see all of your most recent printing errors. (Alternatively, type "Printer" into the Settings app's search bar and select the first option that comes up.) Don't forget that you can print screenshots, too If you need to print from an app that doesn't offer native printing support, such as Messages, screenshots are effectively your best option. Hit Ctrl + Show Display (the function key that looks like a tiny square) to capture your entire screen, or use Ctrl + Shift + Show Display to select the portion of the display you'd like to capture. Once you've got your screenshot, a preview will appear in the corner of your screen alongside a "Share" button. Hit this button to print the screenshot, or go into your files, open the screenshot, and use Ctrl + P to print it any time you want.

item.title: I replaced Google Maps Timeline with a self-hosted app, and it does things Google doesn't offer
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
Google Maps Timeline is one of those features that can be incredibly useful when needed. It can remind you where you went on a particular day, the places you visited on vacation, and even the routes you took from A to B. I never liked the idea of Google knowing everywhere I ever went, so I replaced Google Maps Timeline with a free, open-source alternative that stores location history on my local hardware. I didn't like the idea of Google knowing my every move Google Maps Timeline builds a history of the places you've visited and journeys you've taken, using location information provided by your phone. You can use it to retrace journeys, see places that you've visited, or find when you last visited a specific location. Google is far from the most trustworthy company, and the idea of It storing a history of every place I'd ever been, including my home, work, and daily routines, didn't sit well, so I disabled Timeline a long time ago. Google has since changed how Timeline works. Location history used to be associated with your Google account, and you could access it through Google Maps on the web. Google has moved Timeline data to individual devices in an effort to improve privacy. However, the move wasn't without problems. The original default setting only stored data for 90 days for new users, and a technical issue in March 2025 caused some users to lose their Timeline data completely. It's yet another example of why trusting a third party with your data can easily go wrong. Dawarich is a self-hosted Google Maps Timeline alternative While I didn't want a giant tech company to access my entire location history, I missed some features of Google Maps Timeline. That's why I set up my own self-hosted alternative. Dawarich is a free and open-source location tracker that offers many of the features of Google Maps Timeline. The biggest difference is that while you can pay for a cloud subscription to Dawarich, which keeps all your data in the cloud, you can also self-host it for free. This keeps all of your data on your own servers rather than in the cloud. I run Dawarich in Proxmox on an old Dell OptiPlex, which also runs several other services, such as Frigate and Immich. There's a web interface that I can use to access Dawarich and see my location history plotted on a map, with each recorded GPS point included, and play back journeys at many times the normal speed. I can browse historical dates, examine routes, view statistics and heatmaps, and even use a fog-of-war view that reveals more of the map as you explore. I've also set up Photon, a self-hosted reverse-geocoding service that uses OpenStreetMap data. This translates GPS coordinates into place names, allowing Dawarich to recognize the places I've visited, including stores, museums, gyms, and more. All of this information stays on my hardware, rather than being stored in the cloud. Dawarich can do things Google Maps Timeline can't Google still has the edge in some things Perhaps the biggest difference between Dawarich and the current iteration of Google Maps Timeline is that Dawarich offers a full web interface. Timeline used to, but all the data now lives in the Google Maps app on your phone. It's far easier to examine routes and other data in a browser on a computer than on a tiny phone screen. Dawarich also gives you more detailed access to information; you can view individual location points for GPS accuracy, altitude, speed, and more. You get detailed statistics on distance traveled, time spent in specific locations, and travel patterns. You can also import data from multiple sources, including GPX and GeoJSON formats, and even Google Takeout exports. Google is still better at some tasks, such as identifying where you stopped and how you traveled between stops. Occasionally, Dawarich will mark one of my journeys as cycling, even when I'm in the car. Home Assistant works, but the app is better The Dawarich server is only half of the equation; it can't do anything without location data. Home Assistant already tracks my location and stores the information locally, and I was able to add this data to Dawarich, including several days of historical data. I also use the Dawarich app on my phone, which records location far more frequently. During a short journey, the app recorded 62 location points, compared to just 7 recorded by Home Assistant. This gives me much more detailed journeys, with the Home Assistant data acting as a secondary source. Since the Dawarich server is on my home network, I use Tailscale to share the data remotely from my phone when I'm away from home. The app can store the data and upload it once you're back on your home network, so Tailscale isn't strictly necessary, but it also lets me access the Dawarich web interface when I'm away. While Google Maps Timeline has changed, past events have shown that even if your data is stored on your device, it can still be lost. By self-hosting Dawarich, I have complete control of my data, and with a robust backup system, I'm less likely to lose all my location history.

item.title: Windows 11 promises to clean up bloat, but disabling its own features is the only thing that works
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
Setting up a brand-new computer should feel clean and fast, but modern operating systems treat your personal desktop like an advertising billboard from the second you log in. It gets frustrating watching basic hardware stutter under background tasks you never wanted or asked for. Unfortunately, the best way to make Windows 11 faster is to turn off features it tries to force on you. Why your clean install still arrives full of junk The system stages unwanted software before you even log in When you install Windows 11, the OS comes packed with pre-installed apps, promotional tiles, and cloud-connected features right out of the box. Windows sets up apps in two stages. First they get stored at the system level, and then they get turned on for each user. Built-in apps and pre-bundled software packages start as master templates stored inside the protected system folder at C:\Program Files\WindowsApps. At this point, they're dormant and not using any RAM or CPU. The AppX Deployment Service starts when a new user profile is created or someone logs in for the first time. That's when your PC registers those apps for that user and creates per-user app data folders under %LocalAppData%\Packages. On top of that, PC manufacturers and Microsoft use LayoutModification.json to inject custom app shortcuts, trial software, and welcome screens directly into the Start menu. The promotional stuff goes even deeper than that, unfortunately. Microsoft's Consumer Experience feature connects to its cloud servers during setup, and sometimes in the background, to pull down app placeholders. These are shortcuts for casual games, social media apps, and other software, and it pins them to your Start menu. It does all of that without actually asking you first. Local search is also tied to the web by default. Every time you type into the Start menu or taskbar search box, Windows searches your local files and then sends a request to Bing to grab web suggestions, trending news, and promoted content. This is one of the worst parts of having Windows 11, because the promotional stuff shows up all over the place. I normally see it in the Start menu's Recommended section, in lock screen tips, and on promo cards inside the Settings app pushing Microsoft 365 and OneDrive. These pre-installed apps run background processes, scheduled tasks, and startup entries that eat up your RAM and CPU. All of this adds up during boot and login, and you end up with a noticeable amount of extra disk activity and memory usage. On lower-end devices with limited RAM or slow eMMC storage, cleaning this stuff out makes a real difference. You can clear out the extra junk without breaking anything Basic settings and terminal commands will clear out the files You don't want to try and take everything down all at once. When you clean up Windows 11, you should do it in layers, starting with the easy stuff and working your way up if you need to go further. The easiest place to start is Settings, then Apps, then Installed apps. Sort the list by size or install date to find non-essential apps like Microsoft News, Clipchamp, Solitaire, and OEM trial software, then uninstall them from there. The catch is that this only removes the app from your profile. The underlying template is still sitting in the system image. To stop uninstalled apps from returning every time a new user logs in, you need PowerShell. Running Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online in an elevated session gives you a list of every app template staged in the system image. To permanently remove one of those templates, run Remove-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online -PackageName with your target package name. This is different from Remove-AppxPackage, which only removes the app from the current user's profile. If you run Remove-AppxPackage without also running Remove-AppxProvisionedPackage, the next major Windows update will treat the app as a system feature, stage the files back into C:\Program Files\WindowsApps, and re-register it for every user who logs in. To turn off promotional content and suggestions, go to Settings, then Personalization, and pick Start. Turn off recommendations for tips, shortcuts, and new apps. Also, you have to turn off recently added or opened items. Then go back to the main Settings menu and open Privacy & Security, then General or Recommendation & offers. This depends on your version, but mine was Recommendations & offers. Turn off suggested content, personalized ads, and app launch tracking. To cut off Bing integration in search, press Windows key + R and type regedit. Press enter and go to HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer. If you don't have a Windows folder, make one by making a Key. Then inside, make a Key named Explorer. Right click inside and make a new DWORD (32-bit) Value named DisableSearchBoxSuggestions and set the value to 1. This stops Windows from sending your searches to Bing, so you only get results from your own PC. The last layer is Task Manager's Startup Apps tab (Ctrl + Shift + Esc). Task Manager rates each startup entry by its impact based on CPU time and disk I/O during boot. High impact means the app uses over 1 second of CPU time or over 3 MB of disk I/O. Medium is 300 ms to 1,000 ms of CPU time or 300 KB to 3 MB of disk I/O. Low is under 300 ms of CPU time and under 300 KB of disk I/O. When deciding what to disable, focus on non-essential third-party stuff like update checkers, background chat clients, and browser pre-loaders. Leave anything tied to your hardware alone, like Realtek audio, Nvidia/AMD/Intel graphics panels, and touchpad drivers. Those need to run to keep your hardware working properly. The same goes for your security software. Stripping out system parts comes with real trade-offs Some core packages need to stay in place to avoid system errors Trimming Windows 11 can backfire because Microsoft treats a lot of modern services and UWP packages as core system dependencies instead of the optional extras they pretty much are. You should never remove the Edge WebView2 runtime, Microsoft Defender, Windows Security (Microsoft.SecHealthUI), the Microsoft Store (Microsoft.WindowsStore), or App Installer (Microsoft.DesktopAppInstaller). Leave these alone and go after everything else. Debloating is also not a one-and-done thing. It's going to be a regular part of your maintenance. Windows updates will reinstall any apps you didn't completely remove, so you'll have to repeat the process for those. Take the time to make your PC feel like your own Stripping out system bloat will noticeably speed up an older machine, but it takes some upkeep. I used to think Microsoft would eventually stop pushing bloat and ads into Windows, but I don't anymore. It's just part of owning a Windows PC, but luckily you can get rid of most of it. Spending twenty minutes turning off background noise is worth the time if you want your computer to feel like it's actually yours instead of something you're borrowing.

item.title: Amid Influx of 'Decompiled' Games, New Xbox Lab to Explore AI-Created Ports
item.description:
Source: PCMag
A surge in people harnessing artificial intelligence to reverse-engineer classic video games—including running Halo in a web browser—has prompted Microsoft's Xbox to form a new lab to explore AI-created game ports, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced Tuesday. Some enthusiasts and software developers have been using AI models to efficiently “decompile” classic games, a process that reverse-engineers the game’s computer code into a human-readable format. Doing so manually usually takes years. This has enabled people to port video games to other platforms, including PC, macOS, and web browsers, and even modify the code, raising tantalizing possibilities and questions about retro titles and game development. Although publishers have already issued cease-and-desist letters demanding the content be pulled, it’s not hard to see a future in which gamers privately create and run AI-generated games at home. The same trend is emerging with AI-vibed coded software apps intended to take on legacy products. “In recent weeks, we've seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support," Sharma tweeted today. "Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. “Perhaps more surprisingly, we've seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another,” she added, possibly alluding to a project combining Elden Ring with Super Mario 64. "These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry,” including how games are often exclusive or confined to certain platforms. “While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life, and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models,” she wrote. In response, Sharma is forming a small division called Xbox Labs that’s focused on the vague goal of taking “emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience.” She didn’t offer any concrete examples, but said, “We'll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating. I think Xbox has an important role to play here.”

Here’s how to find the Roku TV that fits your streaming lifestyle. What's the Difference Between Roku Select, Plus, and Pro TVs? All three Roku tiers run the same simple Roku interface, offer the same free streaming lineup, and work with Roku smart home devices. The differences lie in display technology, audio features, refresh rates, which remote comes in the box, and price. - Select Series: The entry-level lineup includes standard LED and QLED panels in HD (720p), Full HD (1080p), and 4K (2160p) configurations depending on screen size, with HDR10+ on 4K models, plus Dolby Audio and 60Hz refresh rates - Plus Series: Stepped-up models feature 4K resolution with four times the pixels of Full HD, QLED displays with Dolby Vision and HDR10+, and Mini-LED backlighting with local dimming zones for sharp contrasts and vibrant colors in a bright room or at night - Pro Series: The theater-quality tier has 4K displays with Mini-LED QLED, Dolby Vision IQ, and HDR10+, plus side-firing Dolby Atmos speakers, a 120Hz refresh rate for silky smooth action scenes and gaming, and a backlit, rechargeable remote Which Roku TV Series Fits Your Room and Budget? For a top-notch experience, you first need to choose a Roku TV size that fits your viewing setup. As a hack, you can measure the viewing distance between your sofa and screen in inches and divide that number by 1.5. That’s a good size to shop. Brightness is another factor. For sunny rooms, a QLED display with Mini-LED backlighting, built into the Roku Plus and Roku Pro Series, uses thousands of tiny backlight zones to achieve massive light output, overpowering direct daylight and keeping colors vibrant. Roku Plus Series 55-inch 4K QLED Mini-LED Roku Pro Series 75-inch 4K QLED Mini-LED What Do QLED and Mini-LED Change on the Plus and Pro Series? Compared to standard LED displays, QLED technology utilizes microscopic quantum dots to boost color vibrancy and deliver higher peak brightness levels that help combat glare in sunny living rooms or brightly lit spaces. Additionally, Mini-LED technology packs thousands of tiny LEDs into local dimming zones to create deeper blacks, sharper contrast, and less halo-glow, optimizing details on dark movie nights. The Pro Series also bumps the refresh rate to 120Hz, which keeps fast action in sports and games looking smoother. What Do You Get on Every Roku TV, No Matter the Series?
